Threat.value: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
I feel on guard even inside my own home

Memory.value: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over
When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop

Negative Appraisals.value: I will never be able to feel normal emotions again
My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe
I can no longer trust my own body

issues.explanation: The threat items are oriented toward external environmental danger (scanning surroundings, planning escape routes), which is hard to reconcile with a life-threatening illness trauma in a 68-year-old policy analyst unless there is an additional trauma context not represented here.

Negative Appraisals: Constant Vigilance reinforces an expectation of unpredictable external danger, which fits assault/combat-type trauma more than illness trauma and does not cohere well with the rest of the illness-based profile.

Memory: Guilt on Recall and Negative Appraisals: Character Blame imply a strong self-blame/guilt formulation, but the other selected items center on current danger vigilance and emotional loss; for life-threatening illness, this specific self-blame pattern is possible but, combined with the external-danger threat items, creates a clinically incoherent mix of trauma themes.

For a life-threatening illness trauma, persistent escape-route scanning is hard to reconcile with the trauma context. It implies imminent external attack or entrapment rather than illness-related threat, while the rest of the profile centers on bodily danger and emotional change.

Intense guilt on recall is not impossible after severe illness, but here it sits awkwardly with the rest of the profile: the appraisals focus on permanent emotional loss and bodily alarm rather than responsibility for causing harm or failing others. The guilt theme lacks support elsewhere in memory or appraisals.

'The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am' suggests a strong characterological self-blame formulation. In a life-threatening illness case, that can occur, but in this profile it is not well integrated with the other selected appraisals, which focus on bodily danger and emotional numbing. Together with guilt on recall, it introduces a self-blame theme that is otherwise unsupported.

vignette: Six months ago, Silas Cole, a 68-year-old widowed African American policy analyst, collapsed behind his mahogany desk during a quarterly fiscal review. A sudden, vise-like pressure seized his chest, and the hum of the D.C. building faded into a terrifying rush of blood. Paramedics found him unresponsive from a massive arrhythmia. The subsequent weeks in the intensive care unit were a blur of gasping through a plastic tube and the cold, clinical certainty that he would not wake up. He survived the episode, but the narrow escape permanently anchored his worldview to the fear of his own physiology. Now, Silas navigates his daily routine with a grim, rigid focus that leaves no room for the dense policy briefs demanding his attention. His body remains constantly tense, a coiled spring waiting to react to danger. Even inside his own home, he feels on guard, pacing the hallway each evening to check the deadbolts and listen for the unnatural creak of settling floorboards. When the conference room vents shudder to life with a low mechanical whine, his breath catches, and he instinctively shifts his posture toward the heavy oak door. He has learned to sit near the office exit, his shoulders locked, convinced that another collapse is merely hours away. He stares at columns of fiscal data until the numbers blur, fully aware that he has lost the ability to concentrate on anything but the quiet dread of impending failure. The past refuses to stay buried, and Silas’s relationship with his recollections has shifted into something alien. When the memory of the ICU returns, he can recall the clinical details perfectly, yet he feels completely numb, as if he is watching a stranger endure those final, fragile hours. The recollection arrives with such visceral immediacy that it feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over. When the sensation peaks, the sheer weight of emotion forces him to stop what he is doing and push his chair back, his chest heaving. This sudden surge of physiological arousal immediately triggers his threat response; the moment the image forms, his muscles clamp down and his heart drums against his ribs, turning the office into a hostile territory where concentration becomes impossible. Silas had come to believe he would never be able to feel normal emotions again, viewing his own physiology as an enemy that keeps reacting as if he is still in danger even when he is safe. Because he can no longer trust his own body, he scans his environment with exhausted vigilance, ensuring his threat response never fully disengages. Yet this constant state of hypervigilance becomes a catalyst for the very thing he dreads: a sudden lurch in his stomach or a tightness in his jaw instantly pulls him back into the ICU memories, which in turn flood him with terror that he is still dying. The more he tries to suppress the panic, the more certain he becomes that his mind and body are permanently fractured. He knows he can no longer trust himself to navigate a simple board meeting without the fear of collapsing overtaking his judgment, a realization that has quietly eroded his standing among his former colleagues. The breaking point arrived when he could no longer sit through a senior leadership briefing without fleeing the room, his hands shaking and his breath shallow. He has scheduled his first consultation with a trauma specialist, hoping to silence the internal alarm that has haunted him since that day behind his desk. Most of all, what frightened him most was the thought that he would never find peace with his own heartbeat, though he desperately hopes to reclaim the ability to simply exist without bracing for the end.
